I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. This is bold, practical action that will cut emissions, bring down household fuel bills and speed the switch to cleaner, cheaper electric vehicles — provided the transition is fair.

We must pair the ban with real plans: public ownership and rapid expansion of renewable electricity, massive home and workplace charging installed by councils, and an insulation drive so families save on energy. For those who can’t afford an electric car, a generous scrappage and public transport alternative is essential — free or heavily discounted buses, trains and bike schemes for young people and low-income households.

This policy is about people, not profits. It stops fossil fuel firms dragging their heels and ensures the benefits of the transition are kept in our communities, not paid out to shareholders. Ban petrol sales by 2030 — Real Hope, Real Change for Fairer, Greener Communities.

Ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030? I oppose it — strongly.

This isn’t about saving the planet; it’s another Westminster edict from the “Green Blob” that hits ordinary working people hardest. Forcing everyone to buy electric cars by fiat will punish families, tradespeople and rural communities who rely on petrol and diesel for work and life. Charging infrastructure is a joke in large parts of the country, and the upfront cost of EVs puts them out of reach for most. It’s a stealth tax dressed up as virtue signalling: higher bills, fewer jobs, and less freedom.

We should be expanding British energy production, scrapping green levies, and investing in practical, affordable transport options — not imposing an ideological deadline that risks driving more people into fuel poverty. If Ministers truly care about the public, they’ll scrap this ban, defend drivers, and let common sense, not dogma, shape policy. Scrap Net Zero to protect livelihoods — stop the war on drivers.

They want to tell hard-working people what car they can buy — and when. I strongly oppose any law to ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. This is an elite, Westminster-driven diktat that will hit families, tradespeople and small businesses where it hurts: their pockets and their freedom.

The truth is simple. Millions depend on petrol vehicles for work — plumbers, farmers, delivery drivers and rural households with no reliable public transport. Forcing them to switch by fiat will push up costs, strand people who can’t afford electric alternatives, and hand more power to the Big Grid and foreign supply chains. All while adding green levies to bills to pay for an expensive, rushed transition that offers little benefit to ordinary Brits.

Instead of moralising and banning, government should drop the dogma, scrap the Net Zero targets that drive these policies, cut the green levies that make energy and motoring unaffordable, and back real British energy production. Let people choose practical, affordable transport without the state dictating their lives. Scrap Net Zero to cut energy bills — and stop the war on drivers.

I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. This policy is about real hope and real change: cutting emissions, cutting household bills, and freeing us from volatile oil markets and corporate profiteering. Electric vehicles are now cheaper to run and, paired with ambitious investment in public transport and home insulation, we can ensure no one is left behind.

But this must be fair. The ban must come with scrappage schemes, grants and interest-free loans for low-income households and small businesses, and a rapid roll-out of accessible charging — prioritising social housing, workplaces and high streets. We also need stronger public transport and free travel for young people, so people aren’t forced to buy cars at all.

For the common good, profits from a renewable-led transition should be reinvested into local communities through public ownership of energy and rail. A 2030 ban is ambitious but achievable — it secures cleaner air for our children, lowers living costs, and helps build fairer, greener communities.

Electric vehicles are now cheaper to run and, paired with ambitious investment in public transport and home insulation, we can ensure no one is left behind.

But this must be fair. The ban must come with scrappage schemes, grants and interest-free loans for low-income households and small businesses, and a rapid roll-out of accessible charging — prioritising social housing, workplaces and high streets. We also need stronger public transport and free travel for young people, so people aren’t forced to buy cars at all.

For the common good, profits from a renewable-led transition should be reinvested into local communities through public ownership of energy and rail. A 2030 ban is ambitious but achievable — it secures cleaner air for our children, lowers living costs, and helps build fairer, greener communities.

I strongly support banning the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. Real Hope, Real Change means acting boldly to protect young people's futures — cutting emissions, cleaning our air and lowering the long-term cost of transport. Petrol cars drive both the climate crisis and eye-watering household fuel bills. By setting a clear 2030 deadline the government can accelerate the switch to affordable electric vehicles, expand genuinely public charging networks, and prioritise investment in home insulation and reliable, cheap public transport.  

This must be a just transition: a ban without support will hurt working families and renters. So action should be paired with grants for low-income households, free or heavily subsidised public transport for young people, and public ownership of charging infrastructure to ensure profits are reinvested in communities. Banning new petrol cars by 2030 is about common sense, not punishment — it’s about building Fairer, Greener Communities where children breathe clean air, people can afford to get around, and our economy works for the many, not private shareholders. For the Common Good, let’s make 2030 the line we stick to.

They want to ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030 — and frankly, it’s another example of the Westminster elite riding roughshod over ordinary people.

Oppose it. Strongly.

This ban is a brutal, top-down diktat that will hit working families, rural communities and small businesses first. Electric cars may look fine in glossy city adverts, but they don’t fix long drives from remote villages, they don’t suit farmers towing equipment, and they don’t come cheap. Forcing people to replace reliable petrol cars with expensive alternatives will drive up household costs, kill jobs in local garages and motoring trades, and trap those who can’t afford the switch.

Worse, it’s enforced climate virtue-signalling by the “Green Blob” while energy bills and taxes soar. Instead of bans, let’s invest in affordable, practical solutions: expand domestic energy, improve charging in the regions, and scrap green levies that drive up costs. Don’t punish drivers — give them choice, common sense and respect. Scrap the ban. Stop the war on drivers. Restore Britain’s freedom to choose.

I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. Real Hope, Real Change means acting now to protect our kids’ future and cut household bills — and this is one of the fastest, fairest ways to do both. Electric vehicles are cheaper to run, and when paired with public ownership of our energy system and investment in renewables, that transition will lower costs for everyone rather than boost corporate profits.

But a ban must come with support for people and communities: funding for rapid home and workplace EV charging, expanded and affordable public transport, grants for low-income households to switch vehicles, and a massive insulation programme so people don’t face new hidden costs. Importantly, we must ensure workers in the petrol and supply industries get retraining and good green jobs.

This policy is about more than cars — it’s about Fairer, Greener Communities. By ending new petrol sales by 2030 we choose cleaner air, secure energy, and a secure future for everyone. For the Common Good.
